days.reason: The day is defined by the Beatitudes (Matt 5:1–12) as a central text. The text describes those who are blessed (the believers who have gone before) and offers hope of resurrection and comfort, which is at the heart of the celebration of all believers.

The text concerning those who are persecuted (vv. 10–12) and the strict ethical demands leading toward the final judgment (vv. 21–48: 'guilty before the court', 'hellfire', 'be perfect as your Father is perfect') are directly relevant to the theme of Judgment Sunday regarding the final judgment and Christ's return.

The Beatitudes (vv. 3–6) describe the inner attitude required for repentance, but the entire chapter (vv. 3–48) challenges the reader to deep self-examination: to abandon anger, lust, hatred, and injustice in order to meet God. This is at the heart of a day devoted to repentance and conversion.

The call to be 'salt and light' (vv. 13–16) and the ethical exhortation to a radically new life (vv. 17–48) are central to the transition from feast to repentance. The text calls for a visible Christian life and preparation for Lent through a deeper righteousness.

The day is defined by the Beatitudes (Matt 5:1–12) as a central text. The text describes those who are blessed (the believers who have gone before) and offers hope of resurrection and comfort, which is at the heart of the celebration of all believers.

The verses about those persecuted for righteousness' sake and the reward in heaven (vv. 10–12) are directly relevant to the theme of Judgment Sunday concerning the final judgment and Christ's return, where actions and faith are rewarded.

The Beatitudes regarding the poor in spirit, those who mourn, and those who hunger for righteousness (vv. 3–6) are central to a day devoted to repentance, self-examination, and conversion, as they describe the inner attitude required to meet God.

The text about being the salt of the earth and the light of the world (vv. 13–16) is relevant for the transition from feast to repentance, serving as a call to live a visible Christian life and bear fruit in the world before Lent begins.

The phrase 'so that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven' (v. 16) points to the relationship with the Father, and together with the context of Jesus' teaching on the kingdom of God, can be linked to the celebration of the Triune God.

_versions.reason: [critical] The link to Trinity Sunday is incorrect. Verse 16 ('...so that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven') concerns God the Father and human response, but does not mention the Son or the Holy Spirit, nor is it a theological definition of the Trinity. Linking this to Trinity Sunday is a forced interpretation that does not hold up theologically. This is a 'false positive'.; [minor] Although verses 10–12 are linked to Judgment Sunday, the entire chapter (especially vv. 21–48) is characterized by a stricter ethic leading toward the final judgment ('guilty before the court', 'hellfire', 'be perfect as your Father is perfect'). The link should be expanded to cover the whole chapter or at least those ethical parts pointing toward judgment, not just the end of the Beatitudes.; [minor] The link to Repentance and Prayer Day is limited to verses 3–6. The entire chapter deals with a deeper, inner repentance (anger, lust, hatred toward enemies) that requires repentance. Especially the sections on reconciliation (23–26) and love for enemies (43–48) are central to a day of self-examination. The link should be expanded.; [minor] The link to Shrove Sunday is limited to 'salt and light' (13–16). The entire Sermon on the Mount is a call to a new life before Lent. There is a strong connection to the transition from feast to repentance throughout the text, not just in the first verses after the Beatitudes.
